title: A Bell for the Smile
premise: Emrys Coldharbour, a late-night radio host, begins receiving calls from listeners who died the previous week — and when every mirror in their house starts lagging one second behind reality, they are pulled through into a mirrored version of their own home where the dead wait patiently to be heard. The dead lead Emrys to a buried truth: in 1974, in this same house, a girl named Wren Halloway was drowned by her family and her death recorded as an accident, and the house has been holding its breath ever since, collecting grief like interest on a debt. To escape, Emrys must return what was taken — not Wren's life, which cannot be given back, but her name, erased from every record by the family who killed her. As the mirrored house begins collapsing inward and the living world starts forgetting Emrys exists, they broadcast Wren's name to the entire county, forcing the town to hear what it spent fifty years not hearing. The house releases them at dawn, but Emrys keeps the radio show, now taking calls from no one at all — because some debts are paid forward, not back.
about_author: Silas Crane is the pen name of a former small-town radio engineer who spent fifteen years maintaining transmitter towers across rural Appalachia before turning to fiction. They write horror about places that remember what people would rather forget.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: POV Emrys. During the final broadcast of 'The Night Line,' a caller describes her own drowning in detail only she could know; Emrys checks afterward and learns she died six days ago. The beat is quiet dread — the first crack in ten years of rational explanations.

chapters.title: The Second Behind
chapters.summary: POV Emrys. At home, Emrys notices their reflection blinks after they do — exactly one second late. They test it obsessively with a stopwatch, telling themselves it's exhaustion. The beat is denial curdling into obsession.

chapters.title: Static Between Rooms
chapters.summary: POV Emrys. Every mirror in the house now lags, and the reflections have begun doing small things Emrys didn't: straightening a photo frame, looking toward the cellar door. A second caller, a man dead for nine days, whispers 'she's under the floor.' Beat: fear becomes compulsion.

chapters.title: What the House Was Before
chapters.summary: POV Emrys, with flashback texture. Researching the property, Emrys finds the house was built in 1973 by the Halloway family, who sold it abruptly in 1975. County records for 1974 are water-damaged, pages missing. Beat: the past has been deliberately made unreadable.

chapters.title: Through the Glass
chapters.summary: POV Emrys. At 3:07 a.m., the mirror over the mantel stops lagging and instead shows the room as it was decades ago. When Emrys touches the glass, they fall through into the mirrored house — identical, dustless, wrong. Beat: threshold crossed, no way back offered.

chapters.title: The Waiting Room
chapters.summary: POV Emrys. Inside, Emrys finds the callers from the radio show sitting in the kitchen, patient and gray, grateful someone finally picked up. They don't want revenge; they want to be heard. One says: 'We're just the echo. She's the voice.' Beat: horror softens into sorrow.

chapters.title: Wren
chapters.summary: POV Emrys. In the child's bedroom, Emrys meets Wren Halloway, eleven years old forever, who has waited fifty years for someone to ask her name. She can't leave the room; she can't even say what happened — the house holds the memory. Beat: tenderness inside dread.

chapters.title: The Family That Stayed
chapters.summary: POV alternating between Emrys and fragmented 1974 interludes. The mirrored house contains echoes of the Halloways — the father's rage, the mother's silence, the brother who watched. They replay the same evening endlessly. Beat: the machinery of a covered-up crime shown without excuse.

chapters.title: Interest Accrued
chapters.summary: POV Emrys. The dead explain the house's economy: every year of silence added weight, and the debt has come due. If it isn't paid, the house will collect from the living — starting with everyone who ever slept under its roof. Beat: stakes widen beyond Emrys.

chapters.title: Return What Was Taken
chapters.summary: POV Emrys. Wren asks for one thing: her name back. It was struck from the church register, the school roll, the gravestone that reads only 'Beloved Child.' Emrys realizes the debt isn't blood or confession — it's recognition. Beat: the theme crystallizes.

chapters.title: Records Burn Both Ways
chapters.summary: POV Emrys. Emrys tries to reach the real world through the mirrors to fix the records, but each attempt costs them something — a memory of their mother, the taste of coffee, the color blue. The house takes payment in identity. Beat: survival begins to price itself out.

chapters.title: The Brother Who Watched
chapters.summary: POV Emrys confronting the echo of Daniel Halloway, now an old man's ghost-loop, who confesses in fragments: he was twelve, he was afraid, he helped carry the bathtub. He begs forgiveness. Emrys refuses to give it cheaply. Beat: anger as a form of respect for the dead.

chapters.title: One Second Late
chapters.summary: POV Emrys. The mirrored house begins lagging too — its rooms arriving a beat behind Emrys's movements, then two, then five. Reality is rejecting the copy. Time is running out in a literal, structural sense. Beat: escalating urgency.

chapters.title: The Living World Forgets
chapters.summary: POV brief cutaways to the outside: Emrys's producer notices missed shifts, neighbors can't recall who lives in the old Halloway place, mail piles up addressed to no one. Emrys is being erased as collateral. Beat: isolation deepens; the cost becomes personal.

chapters.title: Digging Under the Floor
chapters.summary: POV Emrys. Guided by the dead, Emrys pries up the kitchen floorboards and finds Wren's shoes, a hair ribbon, and a child's drawing of a bell — the bell she rang to call her mother the night she died, taken from her hand. Beat: physical evidence, grief made tangible.

chapters.title: The Bell
chapters.summary: POV Emrys. The drawing points to the truth: the bell still exists, hidden in the chimney flue by Daniel. Retrieving it triggers the house's fury — walls breathing, doors relocating, the Halloway echoes screaming their loop louder. Beat: climax approach, the house fights back.

chapters.title: Broadcast
chapters.summary: POV Emrys. Emrys realizes the radio studio exists in both worlds — sound bleeds through. They drag the transmitter's echo into the mirrored house and go live, telling the whole listening county Wren Halloway's name, her date, the truth of 1974. Beat: climax — justice outside any courtroom.

chapters.title: Every Ear in the County
chapters.summary: POV split between Emrys and the waking town. Listeners wake remembering; old neighbors weep; the historical society opens sealed files. Each spoken recollection strikes the mirrored house like a hammer blow. Beat: collective reckoning, power of witness over institutional silence.

chapters.title: What the House Owes
chapters.summary: POV Emrys. With the name restored, the debt inverts: the house owes Wren now. Her echo stands upright for the first time, takes the little bell, and rings it once. The Halloway loops dissolve mid-scream. Beat: release earned, not granted.

chapters.title: Dawn Through Glass
chapters.summary: POV Emrys. The mirrored house folds shut like a book. Wren, fading, tells Emrys: 'You heard me. That was all.' Emrys wakes on the living-room floor at sunrise, half their memories gone but holding the ribbon. Beat: bittersweet return, survival's price tallied.

chapters.title: The Night Line, Continued
chapters.summary: POV Emrys, weeks later. Emrys reopens the records, gets Wren a real gravestone with her full name, and returns to the air. No dead call anymore. But each night they end the show the same way: 'If anyone out there was never heard — I'm listening.' Beat: justice carried forward.

chapters.title: A Bell for the Smile
chapters.summary: POV Emrys, final chapter. On the anniversary, Emrys hangs a small brass bell by the door, and some nights it moves in a draft that isn't there. The last line reveals the title's meaning: Wren smiled once, finally, when her name came home. Beat: quiet closure with a door left ajar.
